What it is:Its  a algorithm which kicks in when react tries to update DOM whenever there is  a state change happening in the component

What it uses: it uses something called as Virtual DOM which is a basically a lightweight copy of actual DOM which is stored in memory

So it compares virtual DOM or new state with virtual DOM of old state. If any changes, it will apply to real DOM

Link:

Reconciliation algorithm determines how the DOM changes in response to any state changes in the components.

It used a Virtual DOM which is a light weight in memory representation of the actual DOM.

It starts by comparing the virtual DOM of the previous state with the virtual DOM of the new state. If there are no changes, it will not make any changes to the real DOM. If there are any changes, it will update the Real DOM to match the new state.

Order in which it efficiently re-conciles:

First, it checks if component type itself is changed, if type changes it will simply unmount and mount new component. Type means from simple text component to a complex component with multiple children

If type hasnt changed, it will compare the properties of the old and new components.

If neither of properties or type changes, it will re-use the existing DOM node for that component which will avoid unnecessary re-renders

Steps in re-concile (RDRU):

Reconciliation algorithm = diff algorithm + handling mount/unmount/update components

Render Phase: When state changes, it creates a virtual DOM.

Diffing Phase: it will identify the differences

Reconciliation: constructs list of minimal changes apply to actual DOM. this is called patch or diff

Update: applies those changes to actual DOM

"Typing" = how a language handles the type of a value (string, number, boolean, etc.) — specifically whether you declare types and when they're checked.

The two kinds

Dynamic typing (JavaScript) — you don't declare types; they're figured out while the code runs, and can change:

let x = 5;        // x is a number now

x = "hello";      // now it's a string — allowed

Static typing (TypeScript, Java) — you declare the type, and it's checked before running (at compile time); it can't change:

let x: number = 5;   // x is locked as a number

x = "hello";         // ❌ error — caught before running

Simple breakdown

Callback Hell:

In programming, callback hell refers to an ineffective way of writing asynchronous code and overusing callbacks. It takes place when you nest functions and create too many levels of nesting. This makes it harder to control access to the specific function and it becomes harder to debug the issues.

Nesting means placing one function in another, placing the third function in the second, then the fourth in the third function, and so on. By placing the callback function in another callback, then again another callback in another callback, in more complex applications, callback logic might get too messy! This type of nesting visually looks like a pyramid which is why callback hell is also called a pyramid of doom.

Components of JS Environment

Call Stack: This is where the JavaScript engine keeps track of function calls. When a script calls a function, the engine adds it to the call stack and starts executing it. If this function calls another one, the engine places the new function on top of the call stack and executes it. This process continues until the stack is empty.

Heap: This is where objects are stored. It's a large, mostly unstructured region of memory.

Web APIs: These are provided by the browser (in the case of browser environments) or other environments (like Node.js). allow JavaScript to interact with external resources and perform operations asynchronously.

Callback Queue(MacroTask queue): When asynchronous Web API operations complete, the callbacks for these operations are added to the callback queue. If the call stack is empty, the event loop will take the first event from the queue and push it to the call stack to be executed.

event Loop: The event loop continuously checks the call stack and determines if there's any work to be done. If the call stack is empty and there are callbacks in the callback queue, the event loop pushes the first callback from the queue to the call stack to be executed.

Macro task less priority over micro tasks. Promise handlers and mutation observers have more priority

Task queue = callback queue

The microtask queue contains the callbacks of operations that are considered more urgent or important, such as promises and mutation observers APIs.

The macrotask queue contains the callbacks of operations that are less urgent such as timers, I/O events, and user interface events.

Middleware — notes

- What: functions that run in a chain between request and response, signature (req, res, next). next() passes control to the next one; skip it and the request stops.

- Flow: Request → [logger] → [auth] → [parse] → route handler → Response

- Used for: cross-cutting concerns — authentication, logging, body parsing, CORS, rate limiting, error handling. NOT the whole app logic (the final route handler holds business logic).

- General pattern, not just Express: also in Koa, NestJS, Django, Rails, and even frontend (Redux middleware). The (req, res, next) signature specifically is Express.

- Lambda: doesn't use middleware/next() — it's a single (event, context) handler that returns a response. Middleware is optional; use Middy (.use()) only if you repeat boilerplate across many functions.

- Why use it (key point): DRY is only a side benefit — you can achieve DRY with plain shared functions. Middleware's real value is the automatic, enforced pipeline: it runs on every matching route automatically (can't be forgotten), can stop a request before the handler, and applies to whole route groups with one app.use().

process.nextTick() = schedules a callback to run immediately after the current synchronous code finishes, before the event loop moves on to promises, timers, or

in other words

▎ process.nextTick() runs right after the current operation completes — before the event loop continues to the next phase.

setImmediate()

▎ Schedules a callback to execute in the check phase of the event loop, i.e. after the current poll/I/O phase completes, on the next iteration of the loop. It runs after synchronous code, nextTick callbacks, and promise microtasks.

So the order is

current sync operation finishes

↓

run nextTick + promises (microtasks)   ← squeezed in BETWEEN

↓

move to NEXT PHASE (a macrotask: timer or setImmediate)

"Next phase" = next macrotask stage

When I said nextTick runs "before the loop continues to the next phase," I meant: before the loop moves on to the next macrotask stage (timers/setImmediate/etc).

Simple summary:

nextTick + promises  → run BETWEEN phases (not a phase themselves)

"next phase"         → the next MACROTASK stage (setTimeout, setImmediate, I/O)

So: microtasks run first (between phases), then the loop enters the next macrotask phase. ✅

So generally how AWS works is, the secret manager is restricted to a region, like it could be in any region like us-east-1 or us-west-1 etc…in my case here we created the secret manager resource in us-east-1 region… So during our internal testing in stage environment, all our users tested the application from east coast so it worked fantastic… But when we pushed it to prod, one user was facing a issue logging into the application, so everyone thought it was a frontend issue/ backend issue (depending on the question blame either frontend or backend)....

Two scenarios:

First scenario:

topics.title: Tell this when they ask, did you take blame for others mistake like that

blocks.v:
Actually it was a backend issue but since the login page was not working, everyone started blaming the frontend code and we as a team were literally digging thru the code to see where it could have possibly gone wrong. But after spending hours eventhough I am a frontend developer I somewhere felt backend was doing something wrong, and I went thru the loggin micro service in backend and I pointed out that in backend the region name where the secret manager was created is not coded… so what it was doing is, when the user logged from west coast, the application checked the secret manager in west coast region but in reality we created secret manager in east coast.. So backend should have coded in search a way that the application should look for secret manager in east coast…so after doing the bug fix, it worked…

So basically I just not only confirmed that frontend is working good, I also pointed out the issue in backend. So I really got appreciation from my colleagues.. Until then I was under real pressure figuring out whats going on bcoz if its failing for all users its simple to debug but if its failing for 1 user out of 100, then its very difficult to identity the root cause.

Second scenario:

Same scenario as above but tell that in frontend code I missed mentioning which region the secret manager was created… so once I added the fix on frontend it started working..

If you are talking as if its someone else’s issue, tell the code fix was done in backend.

If you are talking as if its you issue,  tell the code fix was done in frontend.

To avoid mime sniffing

Consider a scenario where an attacker manages to upload a malicious file to a web server, but the file is served with a text/plain MIME type. Without the X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff header, some browsers might incorrectly interpret the file as a script and execute it, leading to potential security breaches. By using nosniff, you can ensure that the browser will block the execution of the file because its MIME type does not match what the browser expects for executable content.
